fundamentos-produto-agil.title: Agile product foundations for new PMs and POs
fundamentos-produto-agil.excerpt: Start with what matters: the problem, the decision, team alignment, and continuous learning. Frameworks can wait.
fundamentos-produto-agil.problem: New product professionals often hear about Scrum, discovery, and roadmaps before they know what problems they need to solve day to day.
fundamentos-produto-agil.outcome: Learn to explain the problem to your team and show why it matters now.
quickSummary: Agile product work reduces risk before you invest more in building.
Your main job is to improve decisions. Moving cards between columns is only part of the work.
A good backlog starts with clear context. A polished ticket is secondary.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: The team receives a request to "improve onboarding." Before opening several tasks, the PM needs to find the actual problem.
bullets: Which onboarding step is hurting conversion?
Who is getting stuck: end users, operations, or sales?
What will actually change if we solve this now?
exampleScenario.result: Without those answers, the backlog grows quickly and the team may still address the wrong cause.

sections.title: Start with the problem
paragraphs: A framework helps structure the conversation. You still need a clear explanation of the problem.
If you cannot explain which behavior needs to change, the story will be weak regardless of the template.
bullets: Describe the problem in business terms.
Say who feels the impact.
Explain what changes if the team solves it.

sections.title: Use the backlog to make decisions
paragraphs: The backlog should show what deserves a discussion now and what is outside the current focus.
When everything becomes a priority, the team can lose sight of why it is doing the work and focus on closing tickets.
bullets: Separate ideas, hypotheses, and items ready for refinement.
Avoid detailing work too early when it may be dropped.
Review stale and unowned items regularly.

sections.title: Better conversations make teams more agile
paragraphs: Teams work more effectively when product, engineering, and QA can understand the purpose of a change without excessive meetings.
Clear briefs and acceptance criteria let the team resolve more questions before meeting.
bullets: Explain what needs to be validated.
Anticipate exceptions and dependencies.
Bring open questions to refinement before asking for an estimate.

commonMistakes: Confusing speed with productivity and overlooking the outcome.
Opening too many items before understanding the problem.
Expecting a framework to resolve misalignment on its own.
checklist: I can explain the problem in one simple sentence.
I know who is affected and why it matters now.
We have enough context to start refinement without inventing rules along the way.
The team knows how we will tell whether the change helped.

user-stories-na-pratica.title: User stories in practice
user-stories-na-pratica.excerpt: Turn a rough brief into a user story with a goal, expected behavior, acceptance criteria, and questions for refinement.
user-stories-na-pratica.problem: Requests arrive by message, call, or spreadsheet, and the PM ends up manually turning fragments of context into tickets.
user-stories-na-pratica.outcome: Learn a consistent way to structure stories so the team can decide, build, and test with less rework.
quickSummary: A good user story explains intent and behavior beyond the screen or field in question.
Weak acceptance criteria lead to poor estimates and weak tests.
Making gaps explicit early prevents costly discoveries during development.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: Sales asks for company domain validation during B2B onboarding because too many registrations are inconsistent.
bullets: Goal: reduce operational rework.
Story: validate the domain before completing registration.
Criteria: block invalid submissions, keep entered data, and log the failure.
exampleScenario.result: The story becomes a concrete starting point for engineering and QA instead of a vague request to improve registration.

sections.title: Capture context before writing the story
paragraphs: Start with the problem, its impact, the current flow, and the relevant rule before writing the story.
Without that material, a well-formatted story is still guesswork.
bullets: What user or business problem is behind the request?
In which flow does it happen today?
Which rule or constraint must we remember?

sections.title: Describe the intended behavior
paragraphs: The familiar "As a…, I want…, so that…" structure helps when it points to the expected behavior.
If the story describes only a visual component, the team still has to work out what should happen.
bullets: Say who performs the action.
Say what should happen in the flow.
Say why it matters for this problem.

sections.title: Use acceptance criteria to align implementation and testing
paragraphs: Acceptance criteria are especially useful to engineering and QA. They should cover the main path, a relevant failure, and the important exception.
Prioritize criteria that clear up ambiguity about how the feature should work.
bullets: What lets the user proceed?
What blocks the user?
What needs to be logged or preserved?

commonMistakes: Replacing context with a polished title.
Combining several different problems in one story.
Writing generic criteria such as "works correctly."
checklist: The story explains the goal of the change.
The criteria cover the main flow, a failure, and the most relevant exception.
The gaps are stated explicitly and easy to find.
Engineering and QA can use the document to start refinement.

backlog-e-refinamento.title: Backlog and refinement without chaos
backlog-e-refinamento.excerpt: Use the backlog to show what matters now, what needs refinement, and what is ready to build.
backlog-e-refinamento.problem: The backlog grows and changes every week, mixing raw ideas with work that is ready for development.
backlog-e-refinamento.outcome: Use the backlog to focus and refine work so it stays useful over time.
quickSummary: A good backlog shows what is ready, what is still a hypothesis, and what should be dropped.
Refinement reduces ambiguity before implementation.
Refine items likely to start soon.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: A PM has 40 items on the board, but only five are realistic for the next cycle. The team spends time discussing details of items that have yet to be prioritized.
bullets: Separating ideas from items in preparation reduces distractions.
Bringing basic context to refinement saves meeting time.
Flagging gaps keeps the conversation from turning into improvised discovery.
exampleScenario.result: Refinement takes less time and decisions are better documented.

sections.title: Organize the backlog by readiness
paragraphs: Different items need different levels of detail.
Grouping items by readiness prevents premature refinement and documentation rework.
bullets: Idea: still needs context.
Under review: clearer problem, with open questions.
Ready for refinement: enough material for an engineering and QA discussion.

sections.title: Bring enough material to the discussion
paragraphs: The PM should arrive with a goal, known rules, constraints, and open questions.
When everything comes up for the first time in the meeting, the discussion takes longer and covers less.
bullets: Basic information about the problem.
Expected impact.
Known risks, exceptions, and dependencies.

sections.title: Leave with clear follow-ups
paragraphs: Refinement can leave questions open as long as the team knows what they are and who will answer them.
Hiding a gap for the sake of speed only moves the risk into the sprint.
bullets: List open questions explicitly.
Assign an owner to each follow-up.
Keep an item out of the ready column while a critical technical question still depends on assumptions.

commonMistakes: Detailing an item before it has been prioritized.
Using refinement to discover the problem for the first time.
Leaving important questions in the PM's head.
checklist: The backlog clearly distinguishes ideas, work under review, and ready items.
The team's next items already have enough context for a discussion.
Open questions are recorded and have owners.
Refinement helps the team make decisions.

scrum-para-pm-po.title: Practical Scrum for PMs and POs
scrum-para-pm-po.excerpt: Understand what each Scrum event should accomplish so the routine helps the team work with greater clarity.
scrum-para-pm-po.problem: Teams hold Scrum events and still run into unclear priorities, misunderstandings, and rework.
scrum-para-pm-po.outcome: Use each event to make decisions and align the team with a clear purpose.
quickSummary: A useful event clears up questions about the work or its priority.
PMs and POs can help by making the purpose of each event clear.
A meeting that has no bearing on a decision may be doing more than it needs to.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: In planning, the team gets stories without context and ends up arguing over implementation. In the review, everyone watches the demo and comes away without learning from the result.
bullets: Planning should explain what comes into the sprint and why.
The daily should surface significant blockers.
The review should connect what shipped to the problem and what the team learned.
exampleScenario.result: A clear purpose helps the team spend more time on decisions and less on process.

sections.title: Planning: align expectations before discussing capacity
paragraphs: Unproductive planning starts with hours and points before the team understands which work it is taking on.
The PM contributes most by explaining the context, priority, and risks of the main items.
bullets: Which items matter most this cycle?
What is still uncertain or needs validation?
What should stay out for now?

sections.title: Daily: address blockers early
paragraphs: The daily makes blockers visible early enough for the team to act on them.
The meeting loses value quickly if everyone only repeats their task list.
bullets: Which blocker could stop progress today?
Is there a question about a rule, a priority, or an external dependency?
Can the PM resolve something with another stakeholder?

sections.title: Review and retrospective: connect delivery and learning
paragraphs: A review needs context to be more than a demo. A retrospective needs a concrete action.
The PM helps by connecting the work to the problem and bringing real difficulties in the product workflow to the retrospective.
bullets: Did we solve the right problem?
What did we learn about scope, clarity, or dependencies?
What specific adjustment will the team try next cycle?

commonMistakes: Treating Scrum events as proof of maturity.
Bringing work without context to planning.
Leaving the retrospective without a concrete workflow adjustment.
checklist: Each event has a clear decision it should support.
Stories arrive at planning with enough context.
Significant blockers surface early in the cycle.
The review and retrospective lead to specific actions.

seo.description: Use Scrum planning, daily meetings, reviews, and retrospectives to improve clarity, priorities, and learning in product work.

discovery-leve.title: Getting started with lightweight discovery
discovery-leve.excerpt: Test hypotheses about problems and user needs as part of your regular backlog work.
discovery-leve.problem: Teams often make discovery too big to fit into their work, or skip it entirely as delivery pressure rises.
discovery-leve.outcome: Learn a discovery approach that fits everyday work and still tests the assumptions behind backlog items.
quickSummary: Lightweight discovery lowers the risk of solving the wrong problem.
Extensive research can be useful, but most decisions start with an explicit hypothesis.
The goal is a better backlog that incorporates what you learned.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: A manager asks for a new registration field because it "will help operations." Before building it, the PM investigates when the operations team needs the information.
bullets: Who is affected by the missing data today?
How often does the problem occur?
Is there a smaller way to validate the need?
exampleScenario.result: Discovery can show that the problem is in an internal process. Finding that early can save a whole sprint.

sections.title: Start with a small, testable hypothesis
paragraphs: Lightweight discovery starts with a direct hypothesis about the problem, the people affected, and the impact.
A concrete hypothesis helps you ask better questions of users and operations teams and know what data to look at.
bullets: Problem: what is blocking progress today?
Audience: who experiences it most often?
Impact: what should improve if the hypothesis is right?

sections.title: Match the evidence to the risk
paragraphs: Some decisions call for an interview. Others call for looking at the funnel, reading tickets, or observing an operations workflow.
Gather enough evidence to make an informed choice.
bullets: Talk to users or stakeholders who are close to the problem.
Look at basic frequency or conversion data.
Review support tickets, complaints, and operational rework.

sections.title: Bring discovery findings back into the story
paragraphs: Use the evidence from discovery to improve the backlog.
The findings should be visible in the goal, acceptance criteria, risks, and decisions about priority.
bullets: Update the problem statement with what you confirmed.
Record the hypothesis that remains untested.
Turn what you learned into a criterion or refinement question.

commonMistakes: Treating discovery as a separate phase from other work.
Doing too much research for a small problem.
Finishing discovery without revisiting the backlog or priorities.
checklist: The item has an explicit hypothesis.
We have enough evidence for an informed decision.
What we learned is reflected in the story or its priority.
We know what still needs validation before scaling the solution.

seo.title: Lightweight discovery for new PMs and POs | ProdForge
seo.description: Validate problems, hypotheses, and user needs with a practical discovery approach that feeds directly into your backlog.

refinamento-e-criterios.title: Make refinement meetings count
refinamento-e-criterios.excerpt: Arrive prepared, write acceptance criteria that guide engineering and QA, and leave with clear decisions.
refinamento-e-criterios.problem: Refinement has become a long meeting where the team learns about the problem on the spot and lacks the context to decide.
refinamento-e-criterios.outcome: Learn how to prepare materials, focus the discussion on decisions, and leave with specific follow-ups and owners.
quickSummary: Refinement is where you confirm and improve the team's understanding of a problem you have already explored.
Weak acceptance criteria create ambiguity during implementation and leave little for QA to test against.
A useful refinement meeting gives the team decisions it can act on.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: The PM brings an item titled "Improve checkout performance." Nobody knows what improvement means, and the meeting turns into 40 minutes of discovery.
bullets: Which performance metric is falling short today?
For which users is it critical?
How would you measure or observe an improvement?
exampleScenario.result: Without those answers in advance, the team leaves without a decision and the item goes back to the backlog as it was.

sections.title: Prepare the material before meeting with the team
paragraphs: Use refinement to confirm what the team understands about the item.
Bring a goal, known rules, dependencies, and open questions to ground the conversation in specifics.
bullets: What should the user be able to do in the affected flow?
Which business rules affect implementation?
What external dependencies does the team need to know about before estimating?

sections.title: Draft acceptance criteria before the meeting
paragraphs: Draft criteria give the team something concrete to validate, adjust, or challenge during refinement.
"Works correctly" gives the team no guidance. Useful criteria describe what should happen in a specific situation.
bullets: Cover the main path, the expected failure, and the most relevant exception.
Describe behavior: "When X happens, the system should do Y."
Three precise criteria are better than ten vague ones.

sections.title: Leave with decisions and owners
paragraphs: Use refinement to reduce ambiguity around what the team will build.
Give each open question an owner and a deadline before marking the item ready for the sprint.
bullets: List the decisions made in the meeting.
Assign an owner to each open question.
Keep the item out of the ready column while a critical technical answer depends on assumptions.

commonMistakes: Bringing items without context and using refinement to discover the problem.
Writing acceptance criteria after implementation has started.
Leaving refinement with approved items that still have undocumented gaps.
checklist: The goal of the change is clear in one sentence before the meeting.
The criteria cover the main path, the expected failure, and the most relevant exception.
Every open question has an owner and a deadline.
The team can start building without holding another alignment meeting.

alinhamento-com-stakeholders.title: Stakeholder alignment without the game of telephone
alinhamento-com-stakeholders.excerpt: Go to the source of the problem, confirm understanding before writing the specification, and stay aligned throughout the cycle so the review brings fewer surprises.
alinhamento-com-stakeholders.problem: A request changes as it passes through several people. The PM ends up translating secondhand requests without a clear view of the original problem.
alinhamento-com-stakeholders.outcome: Speak directly with the people affected, confirm the expected outcome, and check expectations along the way to reduce surprises in the review.
quickSummary: Alignment means a shared understanding of the problem and what will be delivered.
Speaking early with people who experience the problem reduces misunderstandings in the specification.
A user story helps people align and records what they agreed to build.

exampleScenario.title: Practical example
exampleScenario.summary: Sales asks for a new report and the PM specifies it. At the review, finance says it cannot use the report because a field is missing. Nobody had consulted finance.
bullets: Who actually uses the report day to day?
What decision does the report need to support?
What is missing from the current report?
exampleScenario.result: A 15-minute conversation with the person who uses the report could have prevented the rework.

sections.title: Talk to the people who experience the problem
paragraphs: Each person who relays a request adds their interpretation. By the time it reaches the PM through someone who does not experience the problem, the context has already been filtered.
Talking to the people directly affected before writing the specification is the fastest way to bring useful context into refinement.
bullets: Identify who is directly affected, even if someone else made the request.
Ask what happens when the problem goes unresolved.
Check whether the requested solution addresses the cause or only a visible symptom.

sections.title: Confirm understanding before writing the specification
paragraphs: Ask the requester to confirm what the team will deliver.
A paragraph about the problem and expected behavior that the requester has actually reviewed is worth more than hours of unread documentation.
bullets: Send a summary of the problem and what the team will build before detailing acceptance criteria.
Ask explicitly: "Does this solve what you need?"
Adjust scope before the item enters development.

sections.title: Maintain alignment throughout the cycle
paragraphs: The context and scope may change during development, and stakeholders may come to expect something different from what was specified.
Quick check-ins during development let stakeholders see actual results before the review.
bullets: Show a prototype, draft, or intermediate version before final delivery.
Say when scope changes or a dependency blocks progress.
Check stakeholder expectations before the review.

commonMistakes: Writing the specification before speaking with people who use the product or experience the problem.
Assuming document approval guarantees everyone understands what will be delivered.
Raising scope issues only at the review, when changes are expensive.
checklist: I spoke to the people who experience the problem as well as the requester.
The requester confirmed that the planned delivery solves the original problem.
At least one check-in is scheduled before final delivery.
We communicated scope changes before the sprint ended.

ia-para-melhorar-user-stories.title: Use AI to improve user stories while keeping your judgment
ia-para-melhorar-user-stories.summary: Use AI to organize context, surface gaps, and draft faster. Keep priority decisions in your hands.

como-conversar-melhor-com-dev.title: Have better conversations with engineers
como-conversar-melhor-com-dev.summary: Give engineers a clear problem, rules, exceptions, and constraints. Let the team work through the implementation together.

sinais-de-backlog-mal-definido.title: Spot a poorly defined backlog before it causes rework
sinais-de-backlog-mal-definido.summary: When several stories need an extra meeting to explain the basics, the backlog is missing context.

criterio-de-aceite-vs-caso-de-teste.title: Acceptance criteria and test cases serve different purposes
criterio-de-aceite-vs-caso-de-teste.summary: Acceptance criteria define expected product behavior. A test case describes how to verify it. Keeping both clear helps engineering and QA use the specification.

como-evitar-surpresa-na-review.title: Avoid surprises in the review without another meeting
como-evitar-surpresa-na-review.summary: A surprise in the review often signals late alignment. A quick check-in mid-cycle can save a long adjustment meeting after delivery.
